t: Free Health Calculators: BMI, Calories, Blood Pressure & More
d: 26 free, evidence-based health calculators with formulas and sources: BMI Prime, TDEE, macros, blood pressure, A1C, heart-rate zones, VO2 max, sleep, due date and more.
Calculate your BMI and BMI Prime in seconds. See your healthy weight range, standard and Asian cut-offs, and what BMI can and cannot tell you.
Estimate your body fat percentage with a tape measure using the U.S. Navy formula. See fat mass, lean mass and where you fall in the ACE categories.
Check your waist-to-height ratio, the simple measure of belly fat linked to heart and metabolic risk. Target: below 0.5.
Calculate your waist-to-hip ratio and compare it, and your waist size, with World Health Organization risk cut-offs for men and women.
See your ideal body weight from four classic formulas side by side, plus the healthy BMI weight range for your height.
Enter up to three blood pressure readings to see your average and category under the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline: normal, elevated, stage 1 or stage 2.
Convert A1C to estimated average glucose in mg/dL and mmol/L, or back again, and see whether it falls in the normal, prediabetes or diabetes range.
Enter your lipid panel to calculate non-HDL cholesterol and the total/HDL ratio, and see where HDL, LDL and triglycerides fall. mg/dL or mmol/L.
Check the five markers of metabolic syndrome (waist, triglycerides, HDL, blood pressure, fasting glucose) against the harmonized international definition.
Calculate your maximum heart rate and five training zones, including Zone 2, using the Tanaka or 220-minus-age formula and optional resting heart rate.
Estimate your VO2 max from resting heart rate (Uth–Sørensen) or the Cooper 12-minute run test, and see your fitness in METs.
Estimate your one-rep max from any set of 1–12 reps, then get a load table for every training percentage.
Work out your pace per km and per mile, your speed, and predicted 5K, 10K, half marathon and marathon times with the Riegel formula.
Convert daily steps into distance, walking time and calories, and see how you compare with the 7,000-step evidence.
Estimate calories burned for more than 25 activities using MET values from the Compendium of Physical Activities, your weight and duration.
Estimate your daily calorie needs (TDEE) with the Mifflin-St Jeor equation and see targets to maintain, lose 0.25–0.5 kg a week or gain.
Calculate your basal metabolic rate with Mifflin-St Jeor, the revised Harris-Benedict and, if you know your body fat, Katch-McArdle.
Get daily protein, carbohydrate and fat targets in grams for fat loss, maintenance or muscle gain, with per-meal amounts.
Find your daily protein target by goal and age, plus per-meal amounts, based on the RDA, ISSN and PROT-AGE recommendations.
Estimate how much water to drink a day based on weight, exercise, hot weather, pregnancy and breastfeeding, with cups and bottles.
Add up caffeine from coffee, tea, energy drinks and more, compare with the 400 mg (200 mg in pregnancy) limit and estimate what is left at bedtime.
Find the best time to go to bed or wake up based on 90-minute sleep cycles, so you wake between cycles feeling less groggy.
Enter last week's sleep to see your sleep debt, nightly average and a realistic plan to pay it back.
Estimate your due date from your last period (adjusted for cycle length) or conception date, see how many weeks along you are and key pregnancy milestones.
Estimate your ovulation day and fertile window for your next three cycles from the first day of your last period and your cycle length.
Find out which screenings are recommended for your age, sex and smoking history, from blood pressure and cholesterol to cancer screening, based on USPSTF guidance.
Evidence-based guides to blood pressure, metabolic health, VO2 max, strength, protein, sleep, steps, screenings, nutrition, stress and alcohol.

t: Your 8 Prime Numbers: the health metrics that matter most
d: Eight measurable numbers track most of your long-term risk of heart disease, diabetes and early death. Here are the targets, how to measure each one and how often to recheck.

t: VO₂ max and Zone 2: the fitness numbers linked to longer life
d: Why cardiorespiratory fitness predicts lifespan, what Zone 2 training actually is, and a weekly plan that raises VO₂ max at any age.

t: Strength training for healthspan: a practical starter plan
d: Why muscle is a longevity organ, how little strength training it takes to benefit, and a two-day plan you can start this week at home or in a gym.

t: How much protein do you need? Evidence by age and goal
d: The RDA prevents deficiency; it is not the target for building or keeping muscle. Here is how much protein you need by age and goal, how to spread it and where to get it.

t: Sleep: how much you need and how to get more of it
d: Adults need at least seven hours. Here is what short sleep does to your numbers, the habits with the best evidence and when trouble sleeping needs a professional.

t: Blood pressure: what your numbers mean under the 2025 guideline
d: The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline kept the categories but changed how treatment is decided. Here is how to read your numbers, measure at home and lower them.

t: Metabolic health: the five markers to know
d: Waist, triglycerides, HDL, blood pressure and fasting glucose define metabolic health. Most adults miss at least one. Here is what they mean and what moves them.

t: How many steps a day? What the research actually shows
d: 10,000 steps began as a marketing slogan. The best evidence points to about 7,000 for most adults, with real gains from every extra 1,000 at the low end.

t: Preventive screenings by age: a plain-language checklist
d: Which health checks are recommended in your 20s, 30s, 40s, 50s, 60s and beyond, based on the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, with notes on other countries.

t: Eating for your prime: fibre, plants and the Mediterranean pattern
d: Forget diet wars. The best-supported eating patterns share a few traits: lots of plants and fibre, unsaturated fats, enough protein and few ultra-processed foods.
Stress is not the enemy; chronic stress without recovery is. Here are the practices with the strongest evidence, from exercise and sleep to social connection.

t: Alcohol and health: what changed in the evidence
d: Health authorities have moved from 'a drink a day is good for you' to 'less is better'. Here is what changed, what it means for your numbers and how to cut back.

t: How to read health news without getting fooled
d: A practical checklist for judging health headlines: study type, absolute versus relative risk, who was studied and who paid. Use it on every story in Health Pulse.
